caption:
When you pick "Yes, and don't ask again" in Claude Code, it saves the exact command, passwords included, in a project settings file.
Security firm Apiiro found 1,122 public GitHub copies of that file holding real secrets, and 2,539 secrets in total once old versions and chat logs were counted.
The fix: rotate those keys and keep the file out of git.

Do you check what your AI coding tool saves in your project?

threads_text: Clicking "Yes, and don't ask again" in Claude Code saves the full command, passwords included, in a project file. Researchers found 2,539 secrets from these files on public GitHub, and scanners missed many of them. If you use it, rotate your keys and gitignore that file. Do you read what your AI tools save?

slides.headline: One Claude Code button saved passwords in plain text. Researchers found *2,539 secrets* on GitHub

slides.heading: The *don't ask again* trap
paras: Claude Code asks before running most commands. Pick "Yes, and don't ask again" and it saves an allow rule so it never asks again.
If the command held a password or token, it is saved in plain text in a project settings file.

slides.heading: Pushed to *public GitHub*
paras: Security firm Apiiro checked 104,185 public copies of that file. 1,122 held at least one real secret.

paras.t: With old versions and agent chat logs: 2,539 secrets in 1,994 repositories.

slides.note: Including 379 database passwords and 43 SSH logins

slides.heading: Scanners *missed them*
paras: A password typed into a command looks like plain text, so secret scanners often skip it.
Gitleaks and TruffleHog both missed 215 of the 1,122 files. One company confirmed its exposed key was live.

slides.heading: What to *do now*
paras: Rotate every password or key that sat in .claude/settings.local.json, then untrack the file and add it to .gitignore.
Use secret manager variables instead of typing secrets into commands.

slides.hook: If you code with AI agents, follow so you hear about the next leak before it hits your repo.

site_article.headline: Claude Code approval settings exposed thousands of secrets on public GitHub, researchers say
site_article.dek: Apiiro found that approved shell commands, including passwords and tokens, were saved in plain text in a project settings file that developers pushed to GitHub.
site_article.summary: Security firm Apiiro says it found 1,122 public copies of Claude Code's local settings file containing real secrets, part of 2,539 exposed secrets across 1,994 GitHub repositories. The secrets were saved when developers chose "Yes, and don't ask again" on commands that included credentials.
site_article.seo_title: Claude Code "don't ask again" file leaked 2,539 secrets
site_article.seo_description: Apiiro found Claude Code's settings.local.json saved passwords from approved commands in plain text, exposing 2,539 secrets in public GitHub repositories.
site_article.answer_summary: When a developer approves a command with "Yes, and don't ask again," Claude Code saves the full command, including any password in it, to .claude/settings.local.json. Apiiro found many of these files committed to public GitHub repositories.

paragraphs.text: Researchers at the security firm Apiiro say a convenience feature in Anthropic's Claude Code has led developers to publish thousands of passwords and access keys on GitHub. The findings, dated November 5, 2026, were reported by The Hacker News, Cyber Security News and GBHackers on November 7.
How the secrets end up in a file

Claude Code asks for permission before running most shell commands. When a developer chooses "Yes, and don't ask again," the tool stores an allow rule in a project file named .claude/settings.local.json so the same command can run later without a prompt. If the approved rule is an exact command, any password or token inside it is saved in plain text.

A typical case starts with a developer asking Claude Code to check a database, test an API or troubleshoot a login. The agent builds a command that includes a credential taken from a configuration file, and the approval writes that credential into the settings file. No malicious prompt or stolen account is involved. The exposure happens when the file is committed and pushed to a public repository.

Claude Code adds the file to the developer's global Git exclude list when it first creates it inside a repository. According to the researchers, that protection does not travel with the project, is not added to the project's .gitignore, and does not cover files that were already committed.

Apiiro examined 104,185 public copies of the settings file. It found real secrets in 1,122 of them, holding 1,379 distinct credentials. Counting older versions of files, shared settings files and saved agent conversation logs, the total reached 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories, linked to 63 organizations, most of them software companies.

The exposed material included 379 database passwords, 43 SSH logins for public servers, 23 AWS keys and tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm. The researchers cited a database vendor's admin level cloud key and the owner password for a medical records database. They did not test whether the credentials still worked, but one notified company confirmed its exposed key was live.

Standard secret scanners missed many of the files because passwords written after flags such as PGPASSWORD= or mysql -p look like ordinary text. Gitleaks flagged 564 of the 1,122 files and TruffleHog flagged 643, while 215 files were flagged by neither tool. Of 16 coding agents compared, Claude Code was the only one confirmed to save the full approved command in a project file by default, The Hacker News reported.

No response from Anthropic was reported. The Hacker News said an earlier bug report about plaintext credentials, filed in August 2025, was closed as "not planned" by an automated bot after a period of inactivity.

The researchers advise developers to rotate every exposed credential before cleaning up files or rewriting history, stop tracking the file with git rm --cached, add it to the project's .gitignore, and search Git history for both settings files. They also recommend referencing secrets through a secrets manager and approving command patterns rather than single commands that contain credentials.

The finding shows how AI coding agents create a new class of files that hold sensitive data without developers noticing. Teams that treat .env files carefully may not apply the same rules to agent folders, and scanners built around known key formats are poorly suited to passwords embedded in commands.
The next thing to watch is whether Anthropic changes Claude Code to strip credentials from saved allow rules or adds the settings file to project .gitignore files by default.
